title: Let the one without sin (John 8:1–11)
hookLine: a woman dragged before him; he writes in the dust; stones fall; a passage later manuscripts added

lines: A TRAP: WHAT DO YOU SAY?
cards: Early morning in the temple courts. Jesus is sitting, teaching a crowd. A group of men push through, dragging a woman, and stand her in the middle of everyone.
She's been caught in adultery, they say, in the very act. Moses commanded that such should be stoned. What do you say?
It's a trap. If he says let her go, he seems to set aside the law. If he says stone her, the teacher of mercy approves an execution.
The woman stands there, alone. And Jesus bends down and writes on the ground with his finger.

teach.h: WHAT DID HE WRITE? NOBODY KNOWS.
teach.b: "But Jesus stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground, as though he heard them not." What did he write? The Gospel never says.
Readers have guessed for centuries: the sins of the accusers, a verse from the prophets, nothing at all. They keep pressing.

So he stands and says one sentence: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." Then he writes again. And one by one they leave, "beginning at the eldest, even unto the last."
The oldest first, maybe because they had the longest memories of their own failures. Notice what the story leaves out. The law named both the man and the woman.
Where is he? When they've all gone, Jesus speaks to her directly, maybe the first person that morning to do so. "Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?"
She said, "No man, Lord." "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."

teach.h: NO CONDEMNATION, AND A NEW WAY.
teach.b: Both halves matter: no condemnation, and a new way to live.
A scholar's detail: a modern Bible may print this story in brackets, noting that the oldest Greek copies of John don't have it, and later copies place it in different spots, some even in Luke.

teach.h: LET HIM FIRST CAST A STONE.
teach.b: Some readers think it's an old story about Jesus that circulated on its own before finding a home in the Gospel.
The Catholic Church holds it as part of scripture, and Protestant and Orthodox churches read and preach it too.

how: Christians often read this story when teaching about mercy and judging others; some churches read it during Lent, and "cast the first stone" has passed into everyday English.

games.q: you're one of the crowd holding a stone. the teacher says: let the one without sin throw first. what do you do?
o: argue with him about the law.
games.why: they leave one by one, "beginning at the eldest, even unto the last," until only Jesus and the woman are left.

practice: Think of someone you're holding a stone against, someone who hurt you or failed you; you don't have to forgive them completely today.
Remember one of your own failures, something you'd hate dragged into the middle of a crowd, and if you can, set the stone down, even for a few minutes.
If you pray, ask for help to leave it there; if you don't, notice how your hand feels empty.

wordCard.voice: Condemn. Jesus's answer to a crowd ready to stone a woman: neither do I condemn thee, go, and sin no more.

orig.note: Greek: I condemn, give judgment against. Neither do I condemn thee.

carryVoice: Your line: neither do I condemn you. The stones went down one by one. Go gently.
